editorNote: A telephone giant arrives at the personal-computer counter as printers, graphical software and modem communities widen the meaning of a complete system.
morningLine: AT&T puts its name on an IBM-compatible, while computer owners weigh printers and meet after hours on CompuServe.

lead.headline: AT&T Enters the Personal-Computer Market with the PC 6300
lead.dek: The post-divestiture telephone giant puts an 8 MHz 8086 machine into the crowded IBM-compatible business market.
body: AT&T Information Systems entered the personal-computer market in New York on Tuesday, June 26, placing one of America's largest technology names directly in the path of IBM and the multiplying compatible makers. Its PC 6300 is an AT&T-branded version of Olivetti's M24, built to run software written for the IBM PC.

The machine uses Intel's 16-bit 8086 processor at 8 MHz, a quicker clock than the original IBM PC's 4.77 MHz 8088. Standard configurations offer 128K or 256K of memory, with floppy-disk and hard-disk storage choices for offices moving their work onto microcomputers.

Compatibility is the essential sales argument. Buyers are no longer judging a computer only by its processor or case; they are buying entry to a large library of business programs, peripherals and files. AT&T's national name and sales organization give that argument unusual reach.

The announcement also marks a new direction for the post-divestiture telephone giant. AT&T is not confining itself to Unix minicomputers and communications gear: it is walking onto the same retail and corporate floor as the personal computers changing everyday office work.

stories.headline: Printer Buyers Face a Maze from Dot Matrix to Laser
body: A printer is becoming the costly second half of a home-computer purchase, and COMPUTE!'s June cover package tackles a choice that now stretches from familiar impact mechanisms to laser output. The magazine treats printing as a mainstream concern for homes, schools and hobbyists rather than an office-only accessory.

Dot-matrix machines remain the practical center of the market, balancing speed, graphics and consumable costs. Buyers must still compare interfaces, tractor feeds, letter quality and whether a machine can serve both correspondence and program listings.

Laser printing sits at the far edge of the same conversation. Its presence in a $2.95 home-computer magazine shows how quickly expectations for clean electronic publishing are rising, even while the equipment itself remains outside most household budgets.

stories.headline: VisiCorp Tries to Regain Its Business-Software Footing
body: VisiCorp is trying to reclaim a place in business software after the costly, slow-selling Visi On environment weakened the company behind VisiCalc. A June report describes a broader product line meant to return the pioneer to the mainstream.
The announcements include a floppy-disk-based Visi On Applications Manager. Removing the hard-disk requirement lowers one barrier to trying the graphical system on IBM-compatible machines.

The move comes as Lotus 1-2-3 and integrated packages reset office buyers' expectations. VisiCorp must prove that its visual approach can become an everyday tool rather than merely an expensive glimpse of tomorrow.

stories.headline: Timex/Sinclair Owners Build a Lifeline on CompuServe
body: Timex/Sinclair owners are building an online lifeline after their machine's maker withdrew from the American market. A June users' guide points readers to a Wednesday-night conference on CompuServe's CEM 450 special-interest group.
SYSOP Patrick hosted the weekly gathering, while section 4 of a CompuServe data library carried programs for T/S machines. Byte-Back's ZCOMM software helped owners transfer those files.
The arrangement shows what modems can do for an orphaned computer: scattered owners can trade software, advice and encouragement without waiting for a manufacturer or local shop to support them.

curiosity.headline: Laser Printing Reaches the Home-Computer Magazine
curiosity.summary: A technology associated with expensive office systems had become relevant enough for COMPUTE! to explain beside ordinary dot-matrix printers.
curiosity.detail: The June cover package's title, 'From Dot Matrix To Laser Print,' captures how quickly expectations for computer output were expanding even though laser printers remained far beyond most home budgets.
